rules.statement: Don't ask for the body of an accepted architecture decision record to be rewritten because later code made its claims stale; a newer record that amends or supersedes it, plus an updated Status line naming that record, is enough.
rules.why: Decision records are not edited after the fact: a new record supersedes or amends the old one and updates the old one's status, and the Status, Amends and Supersedes lines are how records relate to each other.
rules.check: Before reporting stale text in an existing decision record, check whether its Status line names a newer record that amends or supersedes it and states the current decision; if it does, don't report it.

rules.statement: In a decision record's Status line and its index entry, cite each related record once, combining relationships into one phrase (for example "amended by ADR-X, which supersedes ADR-Y") rather than repeating the reference.
rules.why: Repeated references read redundantly and are harder to keep consistent when one copy changes.
rules.check: Look for a Status line or decision-index row that links the same record more than once.

rules.statement: Before applying EF Core migrations at startup, compare each context's applied migration ids with the migrations in the assembly, and on an unknown id apply nothing and fail fast with a message that names the context and says how to fix it.
rules.why: When a migration is re-scaffolded, an existing database still holds the old id, so the new migration runs against tables that already exist and fails with a raw provider error instead of telling the developer what to do.
rules.check: In migration-runner or startup code, look for migrations applied without first checking the applied history for ids the assembly doesn't contain, and for missing tests that cover an unknown id.
